## Author’s thesis

Management is presented as the coordinated work of planning, organising, directing, and controlling resources to achieve organisational objectives, but the source immediately complicates that functional abstraction: managerial practice is fragmented, interaction-heavy, verbally mediated, and shaped by responsibilities, hierarchy, stakeholders, uncertainty, and time pressure. [AR] (Ch. 1, “1.1 What Do Managers Do?”; Ch. 1, “1.3 Major Characteristics of the Manager’s Job”)

Effective management therefore cannot be reduced to a single technique. Decisions must fit their novelty and uncertainty; structures must fit environments; leadership must fit followers and situations; motivation varies across individuals; and international management requires sensitivity to both national patterns and within-country variation. [AR] (Ch. 2, “2.3 Programmed and Nonprogrammed Decisions”; Ch. 3, “3.7 Contingency and System Management”; Ch. 4, “4.2 External Environments and Industries”; Ch. 6, “6.4 Cultural Stereotyping and Social Institutions”; Ch. 13, “13.6 Situational (Contingency) Approaches to Leadership”)

The book treats organisations as open systems. External forces constrain and enable action; internal resources, capabilities, culture, people, and design affect how organisations respond; and feedback from performance alters subsequent decisions, plans, strategies, and controls. [AR] (Ch. 3, “3.7 Contingency and System Management”; Ch. 4, “4.4 The Internal Organization and External Environments”; Ch. 9, “9.6 Measuring and Evaluating Strategic Performance”; Ch. 17, “17.1 Is Planning Important”)

Ethical responsibility is integrated into this system rather than treated as an optional supplement. Individual judgement, leadership conduct, culture, compliance, stakeholder interests, corporate social responsibility, and global conduct collectively determine whether organisational performance is responsible and sustainable. [AR] (Ch. 5, “5.2 Dimensions of Ethics: The Individual Level”; Ch. 5, “5.4 Leadership: Ethics at the Organizational Level”; Ch. 5, “5.6 Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)”; Ch. 5, “5.7 Ethics around the Globe”)

Management is finally presented as a continuing adaptive process. Strategy, change, team development, planning, control, technology, and innovation all require learning from outcomes rather than assuming that an initial design will remain adequate. The source states the strategic version directly: “The strategy process is always circular.” [V] (Ch. 9, “9.6 Measuring and Evaluating Strategic Performance”)

## Part I: Managing, deciding, and the development of management thought

### Chapter 1: Managing and Performing

Management comprises planning, organising, directing, and controlling. Planning identifies goals and means; organising designs work and allocates authority; directing influences people towards objectives; and controlling monitors performance and initiates corrective action. [AP] (Ch. 1, “1.1 What Do Managers Do?”)

The functional model describes necessary managerial responsibilities but not the temporal form of the work. Managers move through brief activities, interruptions, conversations, meetings, and information exchanges; communication is not an interruption from management but a principal medium through which it occurs. [AR] (Ch. 1, “1.3 Major Characteristics of the Manager’s Job”)

Mintzberg’s source-attributed classification groups managerial roles into interpersonal, informational, and decisional families. Interpersonal roles establish relationships and legitimacy; informational roles collect and distribute knowledge; and decisional roles turn information and authority into choices, allocations, negotiations, and responses to disturbances. [BT] (Ch. 1, “1.2 The Roles Managers Play”)

The source distinguishes executive, middle, and first-line management. Their emphasis differs: executive managers face organisation-wide and long-range concerns; middle managers connect strategic and operational levels; and first-line managers work closest to employees producing goods or services. [AP] (Ch. 1, “1.3 Major Characteristics of the Manager’s Job”)

Managerial capability combines technical, human-relations, and conceptual skills. Technical skill is most immediately salient near operational work, conceptual skill becomes more important at senior levels, and human-relations skill remains important across levels. [AP] (Ch. 1, “1.3 Major Characteristics of the Manager’s Job”)

The book identifies nine recurring managerial responsibilities: long-range planning; controlling; environmental scanning; supervision; coordinating; customer relations and marketing; community relations; internal consulting; and monitoring products and services. Their relative importance changes with level and organisational setting. [AP] (Ch. 1, “1.3 Major Characteristics of the Manager’s Job”)

### Chapter 2: Managerial Decision-Making

Decision-making is the process of considering possible options and selecting one. Because managers decide on behalf of stakeholders as well as themselves, the quality and ethics of managerial reasoning have consequences beyond the decision maker. [AP] (Ch. 2, “2.1 Overview of Managerial Decision-Making”)

The source distinguishes reflective and reactive processing. Reflective processing is logical, analytical, deliberate, and effortful; reactive processing is rapid, intuitive, and emotionally influenced. Reactive judgement can be useful when expertise allows patterns to be recognised quickly, but it is also vulnerable to biases and inappropriate shortcuts. [AP] (Ch. 2, “2.2 How the Brain Processes Information to Make Decisions: Reflective and Reactive Systems”)

Programmed decisions address recurring, sufficiently understood problems through established rules or procedures. Nonprogrammed decisions address novel, ambiguous, or poorly structured problems and require judgement, information gathering, and the generation of alternatives. [AP] (Ch. 2, “2.3 Programmed and Nonprogrammed Decisions”)

The decision process has six stated steps: recognise that a decision is needed; generate alternatives; analyse the alternatives; select an alternative; implement it; and evaluate its effectiveness. Evaluation feeds learning because an implemented choice may need correction or replacement. [AP] (Ch. 2, “2.3 Programmed and Nonprogrammed Decisions”)

Bounded rationality limits the information, time, and cognitive capacity available to decision makers. Satisficing—accepting an option that meets minimum requirements—may therefore replace exhaustive optimisation. Escalation of commitment can compound a poor choice when decision makers continue investing to avoid admitting failure or losing prior investments. [BT] (Ch. 2, “2.4 Barriers to Effective Decision-Making”)

Additional barriers include time pressure, uncertainty, personal bias, and conflict. The source identifies confirmation bias and seven reasoning fallacies—non sequitur, false cause, ad hominem, genetic, appeal to tradition, bandwagon, and appeal to emotion—as threats to sound judgement. [AP] (Ch. 2, “2.4 Barriers to Effective Decision-Making”; Ch. 2, “2.5 Improving the Quality of Decision-Making”)

Evidence-based decision-making combines available evidence with managerial expertise rather than relying only on habit or preference. Critical thinking, creativity, consultation, and a devil’s advocate can improve alternatives and expose weak assumptions. [AP] (Ch. 2, “2.5 Improving the Quality of Decision-Making”)

Rest’s source-attributed ethical model separates moral sensitivity, moral judgement, moral motivation or intention, and moral character or action. Recognising an ethical issue is thus necessary but insufficient: a person must also judge, prioritise, and act. [BT] (Ch. 2, “2.5 Improving the Quality of Decision-Making”)

Groups can contribute more information, perspectives, creativity, and acceptance than an individual decision maker. Their risks include slower processes, interpersonal and task conflict, groupthink, conformity, suppression of dissent, and uncertainty about accountability. [AP] (Ch. 2, “2.6 Group Decision-Making”)

Away’s decision to print 1,200 copies of a travel book illustrates a small experiment that generated customer demand and helped validate a luggage business which the source reports achieved $12 million in first-year sales. [AE] (Ch. 2, “2.1 Overview of Managerial Decision-Making”)

### Chapter 3: The History of Management

The history chapter presents management thought as cumulative and context-dependent. Early civilisations confronted coordination, record-keeping, logistics, authority, and division-of-labour problems; the Renaissance and commercial companies expanded accounting and administrative demands; and industrialisation made factory-scale coordination a central concern. [AR] (Ch. 3, “3.1 The Early Origins of Management”; Ch. 3, “3.2 The Italian Renaissance”; Ch. 3, “3.3 The Industrial Revolution”)

Adam Smith’s source-attributed account of division of labour connects specialisation to higher productivity. Industrialisation increased both the gains from specialisation and the need to coordinate interdependent work. [BT] (Ch. 3, “3.3 The Industrial Revolution”)

Taylor’s scientific management proposes four principles: develop a science for each element of work; scientifically select, train, and develop workers; cooperate to ensure the prescribed methods are followed; and divide work and responsibility between managers and workers. Its contribution is systematic analysis, while its limitations include an overly narrow treatment of workers and incentives. [BT] (Ch. 3, “3.4 Taylor-Made Management”)

Frank and Lillian Gilbreth extended work analysis through motion studies, while Henry Gantt contributed scheduling and incentive ideas. The source also credits Lillian Gilbreth with bringing psychological and human considerations into management analysis. [BT] (Ch. 3, “3.4 Taylor-Made Management”)

Fayol’s administrative theory shifts attention towards management of the organisation as a whole. The source presents five management functions and fourteen principles, including division of work, authority, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interests, remuneration, centralisation, scalar chain, order, equity, stability of tenure, initiative, and esprit de corps. [BT] (Ch. 3, “3.5 Administrative and Bureaucratic Management”)

Weber’s source-attributed bureaucracy is grounded in rational-legal authority, specialised offices, hierarchy, formal rules, record-keeping, and impersonality. Bureaucracy can produce consistency and predictability, but excessive formalisation can displace organisational purposes and make rules ends in themselves. [BT] (Ch. 3, “3.5 Administrative and Bureaucratic Management”)

The Hawthorne studies shifted attention towards social relations, informal groups, supervision, and employee attitudes, although the source warns that the conventional account overstates a single “Hawthorne effect” and understates methodological and historical complexity. [BT] (Ch. 3, “3.6 Human Relations Movement”)

Barnard treats organisations as cooperative systems whose survival depends on communication, willingness to serve, and common purpose. His zone of indifference describes the range of directives employees will accept without consciously questioning authority when stated conditions are met. [BT] (Ch. 3, “3.6 Human Relations Movement”)

Follett rejects domination as the only way to handle conflict. She distinguishes domination, compromise, and integration, favouring integration when parties can construct a solution that incorporates their interests rather than merely dividing losses. [BT] (Ch. 3, “3.6 Human Relations Movement”)

Systems management treats organisations as open systems exchanging resources and information with their environments. Contingency management rejects universal rules: the appropriate design or practice depends on the organisation’s environment, technology, people, and problem. [AR] (Ch. 3, “3.7 Contingency and System Management”)

## Part II: Organisational context, ethics, international management, and entrepreneurship

### Chapter 4: External and Internal Organizational Environments and Corporate Culture

The external environment includes general forces and task-specific actors that affect organisational opportunities, constraints, resources, and legitimacy. Technological, governmental and political, sociocultural, economic, demographic, and environmental forces can alter industries and organisational choices. [AP] (Ch. 4, “4.1 The Organization’s External Environment”)

Environmental uncertainty depends on both complexity and rate of change. Combining simple or complex conditions with stable or unstable conditions produces four stated environments: simple-stable, simple-unstable, complex-stable, and complex-unstable. [AP] (Ch. 4, “4.2 External Environments and Industries”)

Mechanistic structures emphasise hierarchy, specialisation, formalisation, centralisation, and vertical communication; organic structures use more decentralisation, lateral coordination, flexible roles, and adaptation. Stable environments are more compatible with mechanistic arrangements, while turbulent conditions increase the value of organic features. [AP] (Ch. 4, “4.3 Organizational Designs and Structures”)

The source surveys six organisational configurations: functional, divisional, geographic, matrix, networked or team-based, and virtual. Each redistributes authority, specialisation, coordination costs, responsiveness, and dependence on communication systems. [AP] (Ch. 4, “4.3 Organizational Designs and Structures”)

Matrix structures combine functional and product or project authority, creating dual reporting relationships. They can improve cross-functional integration but also generate ambiguity, conflict, and higher coordination demands. [AP] (Ch. 4, “4.3 Organizational Designs and Structures”)

The organisation’s internal environment includes strategy, structure, systems, people, leadership, capabilities, and culture. The source uses open-systems reasoning and the McKinsey 7-S model to emphasise alignment among interdependent internal elements rather than isolated optimisation. [BT] (Ch. 4, “4.4 The Internal Organization and External Environments”)

Corporate culture consists of shared values, assumptions, meanings, and norms that guide behaviour. The Competing Values Framework distinguishes adhocracy, clan, hierarchy, and market cultures using flexibility versus stability and internal versus external orientation. [BT] (Ch. 4, “4.5 Corporate Cultures”)

Organisational resilience is framed through structural, integrative, and transformative capacities. The source’s nine resilience lenses concern how organisations organise resources, connect across boundaries, learn, improvise, and alter themselves under disruption. [BT] (Ch. 4, “4.6 Organizing for Change in the 21st Century”)

The chapter highlights inequality, geopolitical and social tension, environmental danger, and cyber vulnerability as forces likely to make organisational environments more interdependent and difficult to predict. [BT] (Ch. 4, “4.6 Organizing for Change in the 21st Century”)

A cited virtual-work estimate attributes annual savings of 95,294 tons of greenhouse-gas emissions to telecommuting, equating that effect to removing approximately 20,000 vehicles from the road. [BT] (Ch. 4, “4.3 Organizational Designs and Structures”)

### Chapter 5: Ethics, Corporate Responsibility, and Sustainability

Ethics concerns standards of right and wrong; normative ethics asks which principles should guide conduct; and business ethics applies ethical reasoning to organisational decisions, relationships, and impacts. Ethical dilemmas arise when values, duties, rights, or stakeholders’ interests conflict. [AP] (Ch. 5, “5.1 Ethics and Business Ethics Defined”)

The source uses the financial crisis and Enron to show that ethical failures can impose costs far beyond the offending decision makers. It reports a financial-crisis cost exceeding $22 trillion and an estimated $67 billion economic cost associated with Enron. [BT] (Ch. 5, “5.1 Ethics and Business Ethics Defined”)

Individual values include terminal values—desired ends—and instrumental values—preferred modes of conduct. Ethical reasoning is also affected by incentives, organisational pressures, role expectations, and opportunities to rationalise misconduct. [BT] (Ch. 5, “5.2 Dimensions of Ethics: The Individual Level”)

Seven ethical approaches are presented: utilitarianism; universalism; rights and legal approaches; justice; virtue ethics; the common good; and ethical relativism. They ask different questions about consequences, duties, entitlements, fairness, character, community welfare, and cultural context. [AP] (Ch. 5, “5.3 Ethical Principles and Responsible Decision-Making”)

The approaches can conflict. Maximising aggregate benefits may violate individual rights; formal legality may not exhaust ethical responsibility; and relativism may explain differences without providing a sufficient basis for judging harmful practices. [AR] (Ch. 5, “5.3 Ethical Principles and Responsible Decision-Making”)

Ethical leadership operates through example, communication, reward systems, decisions, and the organisational climate leaders create. Stewardship emphasises responsibility for resources and stakeholders, while servant leadership reverses a purely self-interested hierarchy by placing service and follower development at the centre. [AP] (Ch. 5, “5.4 Leadership: Ethics at the Organizational Level”)

The source identifies five aspects of servant leadership: listening, appreciation, humility, trust, and caring. It contrasts these with a “dark side” of leadership characterised by self-interest, deception, coercion, abuse of power, and disregard for stakeholders. [BT] (Ch. 5, “5.4 Leadership: Ethics at the Organizational Level”)

Ethical culture is transmitted through leadership attention, selection and socialisation, reward and discipline, and organisational stories or routines. Compliance systems matter, but rules without consistent leadership conduct and incentives can become ceremonial. [AP] (Ch. 5, “5.5 Ethics, Corporate Culture, and Compliance”)

Corporate social responsibility expands attention from shareholder returns to economic, legal, ethical, and philanthropic responsibilities. The triple bottom line evaluates organisational effects through economic, social, and environmental dimensions. [BT] (Ch. 5, “5.6 Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)”)

Stakeholder analysis asks who is affected, what interests and power each stakeholder possesses, what responsibilities the organisation bears, and how alternatives distribute benefits, costs, rights, and risks. The source’s framework poses eight questions for identifying and evaluating those relationships. [AP] (Ch. 5, “5.6 Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)”)

The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act discussion reports maximum penalties of $2 million for firms and $100,000 plus up to five years’ imprisonment for individuals. The example connects international operations with both legal compliance and ethical responsibility. [BT] (Ch. 5, “5.7 Ethics around the Globe”)

The United Nations Global Compact’s ten source-listed principles concern human rights, labour, environment, and anti-corruption. The text presents them as a cross-border reference point rather than a replacement for organisational judgement or local legal analysis. [BT] (Ch. 5, “5.7 Ethics around the Globe”)

### Chapter 6: International Management

Globalisation is driven by declining trade and investment barriers, technological advances, and competitive pressures that connect markets and supply networks. Its effects include greater market access alongside greater exposure to economic, political, cultural, and institutional differences. [AP] (Ch. 6, “6.1 Importance of International Management”)

The World Trade Organization is presented as administering trade agreements, providing a negotiating forum, handling disputes, and reviewing national trade policies. The source reports 164 members as of July 2016. [BT] (Ch. 6, “6.1 Importance of International Management”)

Hofstede’s source-attributed framework uses four dimensions in this text: power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, and masculinity. These dimensions describe country-level tendencies and do not determine any individual’s conduct. [BT] (Ch. 6, “6.2 Hofstede’s Cultural Framework”)

The underlying Hofstede study is reported as surveying more than 88,000 IBM employees in 72 countries. The source uses the framework comparatively but also notes that national averages can obscure substantial internal variation. [BT] (Ch. 6, “6.2 Hofstede’s Cultural Framework”; Ch. 6, “6.4 Cultural Stereotyping and Social Institutions”)

The GLOBE project extends comparative cultural analysis through nine dimensions, ten country clusters, and six leader profiles. The project involved about 170 researchers and data from approximately 17,000 managers in 62 countries. [BT] (Ch. 6, “6.3 The GLOBE Framework”)

Cultural stereotyping mistakes a group-level tendency for a reliable prediction about an individual. The source reports that approximately 80% of cultural variation occurs within countries, supporting contextual inquiry over rigid national typing. [BT] (Ch. 6, “6.4 Cultural Stereotyping and Social Institutions”)

Social stratification, education, and religion are treated as institutions that influence work, authority, opportunity, consumption, and organisational legitimacy. These institutions interact with culture rather than operating as interchangeable measures of it. [AP] (Ch. 6, “6.4 Cultural Stereotyping and Social Institutions”)

Cultural intelligence combines cognitive knowledge, metacognitive awareness, motivation, and behavioural capability. Cross-cultural competence therefore requires learning, reflection, willingness to engage, and the capacity to adapt behaviour. [AP] (Ch. 6, “6.5 Cross-Cultural Assignments”)

The source distinguishes lower-rigour and higher-rigour cross-cultural training and locates training before and after arrival. It recommends predeparture preparation roughly three to five weeks before departure and post-arrival training approximately eight to twelve weeks after arrival. [BT] (Ch. 6, “6.5 Cross-Cultural Assignments”)

International strategy may emphasise global standardisation, regional coordination, or local adaptation. Pure forms are uncommon; firms may combine approaches across products, regions, and functions. [AP] (Ch. 6, “6.6 Strategies for Expanding Globally”)

Market-entry modes include exporting, licensing or franchising, strategic alliances, and foreign direct investment. Increasing commitment can offer greater control and learning while exposing the firm to greater cost, risk, and institutional dependence. [AP] (Ch. 6, “6.7 The Necessity of Global Markets”)

The Uppsala model depicts gradual internationalisation through accumulated knowledge and commitment, whereas born-global firms internationalise early. The source cites an analysis finding only nine companies among the Fortune Global 500 that qualified as truly global under the study’s criteria. [BT] (Ch. 6, “6.7 The Necessity of Global Markets”)

### Chapter 7: Entrepreneurship

Entrepreneurship is the recognition and pursuit of an opportunity through the creation or transformation of an organisation. The source distinguishes classic entrepreneurs, multipreneurs who create several ventures, and intrapreneurs who innovate within established organisations. [AP] (Ch. 7, “7.1 Entrepreneurship”)

Nine characteristics are associated with successful entrepreneurs: ambition, independence, self-confidence, willingness to take moderate risks, vision, creativity, energy, passion, and commitment. The chapter presents these as tendencies and developable capacities, not a deterministic personality test. [AP] (Ch. 7, “7.2 Characteristics of Successful Entrepreneurs”)

Small businesses contribute about half of U.S. economic output and employ about half of the private-sector workforce. The source cautions that estimates of the number of small firms vary because definitions use different employee, revenue, industry, and ownership criteria. [BT] (Ch. 7, “7.3 Small Business”)

The Kauffman Foundation’s entrepreneurship measures are organised into three indexes covering start-up activity, main-street entrepreneurship, and growth entrepreneurship. [BT] (Ch. 7, “7.3 Small Business”)

The source reports that approximately 75% of start-ups are newly created, while roughly 25% arise through buying an existing business or franchise. It also reports that 94% of entrepreneurs use personal savings or money from family and friends. [BT] (Ch. 7, “7.4 Start Your Own Business”)

A business plan integrates the product or service, market, competitive environment, operating arrangements, management, risks, and financial projections. Its value lies in testing assumptions and coordinating action as well as seeking finance. [AP] (Ch. 7, “7.4 Start Your Own Business”)

Funding sources include personal funds, debt, trade credit, angel investors, venture capital, and government-supported finance. The source reports that three-quarters of Inc. 500 founders began with no more than $100,000 and that equity investors may seek ownership stakes of 65–75%. [BT] (Ch. 7, “7.4 Start Your Own Business”)

Nearly half of new businesses fail within five years. The chapter associates failure with economic conditions, inadequate capital, high costs, insufficient experience, weak planning, and personal decisions, while also warning that growth itself can strain cash, systems, and managerial capacity. [BT] (Ch. 7, “7.4 Start Your Own Business”; Ch. 7, “7.5 Managing a Small Business”)

Small firms can prosper through proximity to customers, speed, flexibility, niche focus, innovation, lower overhead, and personal service. These advantages coexist with limited finance, concentrated risk, dependence on owners, and difficulty acquiring specialised capability. [AP] (Ch. 7, “7.6 The Large Impact of Small Business”)

The Small Business Administration provides information, counselling, contracting assistance, and support for finance and international trade. Export trading companies and export management companies may charge fees of approximately 5–15% for export-related services. [BT] (Ch. 7, “7.7 The Small Business Administration”)

Felecia Hatcher’s work addressing “innovation deserts” illustrates entrepreneurship directed towards widening access to technology, mentoring, and venture opportunities in underserved communities. [AE] (Ch. 7, “7.8 Trends in Entrepreneurship and Small-Business Ownership”)

## Part III: Strategic analysis, strategic management, and organisational change

### Chapter 8: Strategic Analysis

Strategic analysis is the systematic examination of a firm’s competitive environment. It connects external opportunities and threats with internal strengths, weaknesses, resources, and capabilities so that strategy rests on evidence about the firm and its setting. [AP] (Ch. 8, “8.1 Gaining Advantages by Understanding the Competitive Environment”)

SWOT separates internal strengths and weaknesses from external opportunities and threats. Its accessibility is also a limitation: categories can become broad, subjective, and dependent on the analyst unless supported by deeper environmental and internal analysis. [AR] (Ch. 8, “8.2 Using SWOT for Strategic Analysis”)

PESTEL examines six macro-environmental domains: political, economic, sociocultural, technological, environmental, and legal. These domains can overlap, and a change in one may propagate through several others. [AP] (Ch. 8, “8.3 A Firm’s External Macro Environment: PESTEL”)

Porter’s Five Forces analyses industry rivalry, threat of new entrants, substitutes, supplier power, and buyer power. The forces influence industry attractiveness and the share of value available to firms, suppliers, customers, entrants, and substitutes. [BT] (Ch. 8, “8.4 A Firm’s Micro Environment: Porter’s Five Forces”)

Internal analysis distinguishes resources—assets the firm controls—from capabilities—its ability to deploy resources through coordinated activity. Value-chain analysis separates primary activities from supporting activities to identify where value, cost, coordination, or differentiation arise. [AP] (Ch. 8, “8.5 The Internal Environment”)

VRIO tests whether a resource or capability is valuable, rare, difficult to imitate, and supported by the organisation. Passing only some tests may create competitive parity or temporary advantage rather than a sustained advantage. [BT] (Ch. 8, “8.5 The Internal Environment”)

Strategy is a pattern of planned and implemented actions intended to produce success in competition. Competitive advantage exists when a firm creates greater value or performs in a way competitors cannot readily reproduce. [AP] (Ch. 8, “8.6 Competition, Strategy, and Competitive Advantage”)

Porter’s three generic business-level strategies are cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. Cost leadership seeks a lower cost position; differentiation creates valued distinctiveness; focus narrows the competitive scope and then competes through cost or differentiation within it. [BT] (Ch. 8, “8.6 Competition, Strategy, and Competitive Advantage”)

Strategic positioning specifies how the firm competes, whom it serves, and where it operates. A defensible position is internally coherent and difficult to imitate rather than merely a slogan or isolated product feature. [AP] (Ch. 8, “8.7 Strategic Positioning”)

### Chapter 9: The Strategic Management Process

Strategic management is a cycle involving vision and mission, strategic analysis, objectives, strategy formulation, implementation, and performance evaluation. Although presented as distinguishable activities, these processes overlap and continually inform one another. [AP] (Ch. 9, “9.1 Strategic Management”; Ch. 9, “9.6 Measuring and Evaluating Strategic Performance”)

A vision states a desired future and broad organisational purpose; a mission identifies the business, products or services, markets, and approach through which the organisation pursues that future. [AP] (Ch. 9, “9.2 Firm Vision and Mission”)

Strategic analysis informs strategy but does not mechanically select it. Managers interpret environmental and organisational evidence, make trade-offs, and choose a position under uncertainty. [AR] (Ch. 9, “9.3 The Role of Strategic Analysis in Formulating a Strategy”)

The source distinguishes business-level, corporate-level, and international strategy. Business strategy concerns competition within an industry; corporate strategy governs the organisation’s portfolio and scope; and international strategy addresses competition and coordination across countries. [AP] (Ch. 9, “9.4 Strategic Objectives and Levels of Strategy”)

Grand strategies are grouped as growth, stability, and defensive strategies. Growth expands activity; stability maintains the current direction; and defensive strategies retrench, restructure, divest, or otherwise respond to weak performance or threat. [AP] (Ch. 9, “9.4 Strategic Objectives and Levels of Strategy”)

Strategic objectives translate broad direction into targeted results. The SMART framework tests whether objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. [AP] (Ch. 9, “9.4 Strategic Objectives and Levels of Strategy”)

Planning occurs at strategic, tactical, and operational levels. Short-term plans generally cover one year or less, while long-term strategic plans extend beyond one year; their value depends on alignment rather than duration alone. [AP] (Ch. 9, “9.5 Planning Firm Actions to Implement Strategies”)

Implementation turns chosen strategy into structures, resource allocations, policies, projects, incentives, and operating behaviour. A strategy that is not translated into coordinated action remains an intention rather than an organisational result. [AR] (Ch. 9, “9.5 Planning Firm Actions to Implement Strategies”)

Performance measurement compares results with objectives and benchmarks. Feedback may validate the strategy, reveal implementation problems, or change the assumptions used in the next strategic analysis: “The strategy process is always circular.” [V] (Ch. 9, “9.6 Measuring and Evaluating Strategic Performance”)

Interface’s sustainability programme illustrates strategy translated into seven operational fronts: eliminating waste, making emissions benign, using renewable energy, closing material loops, improving transport efficiency, sensitising stakeholders, and redesigning commerce. [AE] (Ch. 9, “9.5 Planning Firm Actions to Implement Strategies”)

### Chapter 10: Organizational Structure and Change

Organisational structure specifies formal roles, authority, division of labour, reporting relationships, and coordination. Informal relationships coexist with the formal organisation and can either support or frustrate its design. [AP] (Ch. 10, “10.1 Organizational Structures and Design”)

The source’s treatment of Weberian bureaucracy identifies five design elements: specialisation, command-and-control hierarchy, span of control, centralisation, and formalisation. Their configuration helps place an organisation on a continuum between mechanistic and organic design. [BT] (Ch. 10, “10.1 Organizational Structures and Design”)

Vertical structures emphasise hierarchical authority, while horizontal designs organise more activity around processes, teams, or lateral relationships. Product, geographic, and matrix structures respond to different needs for specialisation and integration. [AP] (Ch. 10, “10.1 Organizational Structures and Design”)

Organisational change may be structural, technological, or cultural. These categories interact: adopting technology can alter jobs and authority, while structural change can require new cultural expectations. [AP] (Ch. 10, “10.2 Organizational Change”)

The organisational life cycle has four stated phases: entrepreneurship, survival and early success, sustained success or maturity, and renewal or decline. Growth creates new coordination and control requirements rather than simply enlarging an unchanged organisation. [AP] (Ch. 10, “10.2 Organizational Change”)

Change varies across three dimensions: scope, level, and intentionality. Scope ranges from incremental through strategic to transformational change; level may be individual, group, or organisational; and change may be planned or unplanned. [AP] (Ch. 10, “10.2 Organizational Change”)

Deficit-based change starts from a problem or gap, while abundance-based change starts from strengths and possibilities. Top-down change relies on senior direction; bottom-up or emergent change mobilises participation and local knowledge. The source treats these as assumptions and choices, not mutually exclusive doctrines. [AR] (Ch. 10, “10.3 Managing Change”)

Lewin’s model has three phases: unfreezing the current state, changing, and refreezing new practices. [BT] (Ch. 10, “10.3 Managing Change”)

Kotter’s model identifies eight steps: establish urgency; form a guiding coalition; create a vision; communicate it; remove obstacles; generate short-term wins; consolidate improvements; and anchor change in culture. [BT] (Ch. 10, “10.3 Managing Change”)

David Cooperrider’s source-attributed Appreciative Inquiry model uses five “D” activities: define, discover, dream, design, and destiny. It directs inquiry towards strengths and desired possibilities rather than beginning solely with deficits. [BT] (Ch. 10, “10.3 Managing Change”)

Complex adaptive systems approaches focus on agents, connections, information flows, boundary conditions, disturbances, and interactions capable of producing transformation. Open Space Technology is presented as one way to enable self-organising conversation around important issues. [BT] (Ch. 10, “10.3 Managing Change”)

The chapter does not select one universally superior change model. Change assumptions and methods should fit the type of change, organisational context, readiness, participation needs, and uncertainty involved. [AR] (Ch. 10, “10.3 Managing Change”)

## Part IV: Human resources, diversity, and leadership

### Chapter 11: Human Resource Management

Human resource management aligns the organisation’s need for capability with the employee life cycle, legal obligations, performance systems, rewards, talent acquisition, and development. It is presented as a shared responsibility between HR specialists and managers. [AR] (Ch. 11, “11.1 An Introduction to Human Resource Management”)

The source describes four waves of HR development: administrative work; design of innovative HR practices; integration with business strategy; and an “outside-in” orientation connecting HR to customers, investors, communities, and external conditions. [BT] (Ch. 11, “11.1 An Introduction to Human Resource Management”)

Five key areas organise the employee life cycle: compliance; selection, hiring, and onboarding; performance management; rewards and benefits; and talent development or succession. [AP] (Ch. 11, “11.1 An Introduction to Human Resource Management”)

The compliance discussion identifies six major U.S. laws: the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, Fair Labor Standards Act, Family and Medical Leave Act, National Labor Relations Act, and Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act. Training, documentation, consistent practice, and auditing support compliance. [AP] (Ch. 11, “11.2 Human Resource Management and Compliance”)

Performance management aligns expectations, goals, feedback, evaluation, development, and consequences. The source contrasts this continuous process with an annual appraisal treated as an isolated administrative event. [AP] (Ch. 11, “11.3 Performance Management”)

Forced-ranking systems can create internal competition and weaken collaboration. The source reports that GE abandoned forced ranking and cites Deloitte’s finding that 58% of executives believed their current performance-management approach drove neither engagement nor high performance. [BT] (Ch. 11, “11.3 Performance Management”)

Performance-management challenges include aligning individual and organisational goals, distinguishing levels of contribution, rewarding appropriately, addressing poor performance, maintaining legal defensibility, and preventing feedback from becoming an unmanageable “fire hose.” [AP] (Ch. 11, “11.3 Performance Management”)

Pay-for-performance links rewards to results but requires credible measures, employee influence over outcomes, differentiated rewards, and transparent administration. Total rewards comprises six components: compensation, benefits, work-life effectiveness, recognition, performance management, and talent development. [AP] (Ch. 11, “11.4 Influencing Employee Performance and Motivation”)

The four-drive model describes drives to acquire, bond, comprehend, and defend. The source uses it to argue that a single reward mechanism cannot fully motivate employees because different organisational practices address different drives. [BT] (Ch. 11, “11.4 Influencing Employee Performance and Motivation”)

Talent acquisition anticipates capability needs, specifies roles, creates candidate pools, assesses candidates, closes the hire, integrates the person, and reviews outcomes. Recruitment quality depends on both selection and the organisation’s ability to attract and retain suitable candidates. [AP] (Ch. 11, “11.5 Building an Organization for the Future”)

The 9-box framework combines performance and potential to support talent discussion. The source lists six potential indicators and warns that talent judgements need calibration rather than reliance on one manager’s unexamined view. [AP] (Ch. 11, “11.6 Talent Development and Succession Planning”)

Succession planning considers candidates ready in less than one year, one to three years, or more than three years, while retaining external recruitment as an option. Development responses include training, stretch assignments, assessment, mentoring, and individual development plans. [AP] (Ch. 11, “11.6 Talent Development and Succession Planning”)

### Chapter 12: Diversity in Organizations

Diversity concerns identity-based differences among people, while inclusion concerns whether people can participate, contribute, and belong. Managing diversity means shaping organisational systems and relationships so that differences do not become arbitrary barriers. [AP] (Ch. 12, “12.1 An Introduction to Workplace Diversity”)

The source distinguishes surface-level diversity, deep-level diversity, and hidden diversity. Surface characteristics are more immediately observable; deep-level differences include values and attitudes; hidden identities may be invisible unless disclosed. [AP] (Ch. 12, “12.1 An Introduction to Workplace Diversity”)

The workforce discussion covers sex and gender, race and ethnicity, age, sexual orientation, immigration status, disability, and religion. Its demographic and legal statistics are principally U.S.-specific and frequently derive from dated government or survey sources identified in the chapter. [AP] (Ch. 12, “12.2 Diversity and the Workforce”)

Sexual harassment is divided into quid pro quo and hostile-work-environment forms. The first conditions employment consequences on sexual conduct; the second concerns conduct sufficiently severe or pervasive to alter working conditions. [BT] (Ch. 12, “12.2 Diversity and the Workforce”)

The business case for diversity identifies six opportunities: cost advantages, improved resource acquisition, marketing advantages, system flexibility, greater creativity, and better problem-solving. These are opportunities contingent on organisational practice rather than automatic effects of demographic variety. [BT] (Ch. 12, “12.3 Diversity and Its Impact on Companies”)

Strategic human resource management can align diversity with organisational goals. The resource-based view asks whether diversity-related capabilities are valuable, rare, difficult to imitate, and non-substitutable, but the source reports mixed evidence concerning direct diversity–performance relationships. [BT] (Ch. 12, “12.3 Diversity and Its Impact on Companies”)

Challenges include lower attachment among dissimilar employees, stereotyping, exclusion, interpersonal conflict, discrimination, unequal access, and unequal treatment. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission categories described include age, disability, national origin, pregnancy, race or colour, religion, and sex-based discrimination. [AP] (Ch. 12, “12.4 Challenges of Diversity”)

The cognitive-diversity hypothesis proposes that differing perspectives can improve information processing and problem-solving. Similarity-attraction predicts greater interpersonal attraction among people perceived as similar. Social identity theory explains categorisation into in-groups and out-groups. [BT] (Ch. 12, “12.5 Key Diversity Theories”)

Schema theory explains how organised cognitive categories shape perception, while the justification-suppression model explains how prejudice may be restrained or expressed depending on available justifications and social pressures. [BT] (Ch. 12, “12.5 Key Diversity Theories”)

Three diversity perspectives are distinguished: integration-and-learning, access-and-legitimacy, and discrimination-and-fairness. Integration-and-learning connects differences to core work and learning; access-and-legitimacy uses diversity to reach constituencies; discrimination-and-fairness emphasises equal treatment and representation. [BT] (Ch. 12, “12.6 Benefits and Challenges of Workplace Diversity”)

Recommended practices include structured recruitment and interviews, diversified mentoring, visible leadership accountability, meaningful training, fair evaluation, and integration of inclusion into ordinary management systems. The source lists fifteen characteristics of highly structured interviews. [AP] (Ch. 12, “12.7 Recommendations for Managing Diversity”)

### Chapter 13: Leadership

Leadership is interpersonal influence between people who depend on one another to achieve mutual purposes. The source distinguishes leadership from management without treating them as mutually exclusive: managers hold formal appointments, while leaders may emerge through acceptance and influence. [AP] (Ch. 13, “13.1 The Nature of Leadership”)

The leadership process contains five interacting components: leader, followers, context, influence process, and outcomes. Leader–member exchange theory emphasises that leaders develop relationships of differing quality with individual followers. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.2 The Leadership Process”)

Formal leaders occupy designated positions; informal leaders influence others without necessarily holding formal authority. Emergence depends on personal attributes, behaviour, group needs, and the surrounding situation. [AP] (Ch. 13, “13.3 Leader Emergence”)

French and Raven’s source-attributed framework identifies reward, coercive, referent, expert, and legitimate power. The source reports more favourable responses to referent and expert power and to reasoned influence, while coercion can produce resistance and alienation. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.3 Leader Emergence”)

The Tannenbaum–Schmidt continuum places leader-centred and follower-centred behaviour along a range rather than reducing leadership to one fixed style. McGregor’s Theory X and Theory Y contrast assumptions about whether workers avoid responsibility or can exercise self-direction and commitment. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.4 The Trait Approach to Leadership”)

The trait approach associates leadership with drive, motivation, honesty and integrity, self-confidence, cognitive ability, and knowledge of the business, among other characteristics. The source rejects the inference that traits alone guarantee leadership effectiveness. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.4 The Trait Approach to Leadership”)

Behavioural approaches include Ohio State’s consideration and initiating structure, Michigan’s employee- and production-centred orientations, and the managerial grid. Research does not establish one combination as universally superior across all settings. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.5 Behavioral Approaches to Leadership”)

Fiedler’s contingency model uses least-preferred-coworker orientation and three situational factors—leader–member relations, task structure, and position power—to examine fit between style and situation. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.6 Situational (Contingency) Approaches to Leadership”)

Path–goal theory identifies supportive, directive, participative, and achievement-oriented leader behaviours. Leadership should clarify paths, remove obstacles, and connect performance with valued outcomes in a manner suited to follower and task characteristics. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.6 Situational (Contingency) Approaches to Leadership”)

Cross-cultural evidence further limits universal claims: “There appears to be consensus that a universal approach to leadership and leader effectiveness does not exist.” [V] (Ch. 13, “13.6 Situational (Contingency) Approaches to Leadership”)

Substitutes for leadership can make direct leader intervention unnecessary, while neutralisers can prevent a leader from influencing outcomes. Follower capability, intrinsically satisfying work, cohesive groups, formal rules, and spatial distance can alter the need or opportunity for leadership. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.7 Substitutes for and Neutralizers of Leadership”)

Transactional leadership exchanges rewards or corrective action for performance. Transformational leadership works through charisma, individualised consideration, intellectual stimulation, and inspirational motivation; charismatic influence can produce exceptional commitment but also concentrates risks when followers suspend judgement. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.8 Transformational, Visionary, and Charismatic Leadership”)

The source’s twenty-first-century leadership profile calls for strategic opportunism, global awareness, decentralised authority, sensitivity to diversity, interpersonal competence, and community-building. [BT] (Ch. 13, “13.9 Leadership Needs in the 21st Century”)

## Part V: Motivation, teams, and communication

### Chapter 14: Work Motivation for Performance

Job performance depends on four determinants: ability, role perceptions, the performance environment, and motivation. Motivation supplies direction—what behaviour is chosen—and intensity—how much effort is applied. [AP] (Ch. 14, “14.1 Motivation: Direction and Intensity”)

Content theories examine what needs motivate people; process theories examine how people choose, sustain, and revise motivated behaviour. The source presents multiple theories because no single account explains every person and setting. [AR] (Ch. 14, “14.1 Motivation: Direction and Intensity”)

Murray distinguishes primary and secondary needs and manifest and latent needs. McClelland’s learned-needs theory concentrates on achievement, affiliation, and power; the source further distinguishes personalised from socialised power. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.2 Content Theories of Motivation”)

Maslow’s hierarchy contains physiological, safety, social, esteem, and self-actualisation needs. The source reports that research does not support a rigid universal sequence in which one level must be fully satisfied before another becomes active. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.2 Content Theories of Motivation”)

Alderfer’s ERG theory groups needs into existence, relatedness, and growth and allows several needs to operate simultaneously. It adds satisfaction progression, frustration, frustration regression, and aspiration as possible dynamics. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.2 Content Theories of Motivation”)

Herzberg distinguishes motivators associated with work content from hygiene factors associated with work context. The source notes that calling this a “two-factor theory” can misleadingly imply only two individual factors rather than two larger sets. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.2 Content Theories of Motivation”)

Self-determination theory centres competence, autonomy, and relatedness. It distinguishes intrinsic from extrinsic motivation and warns that poorly designed external rewards can reduce intrinsic motivation. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.2 Content Theories of Motivation”)

The four process theories covered are operant conditioning, equity, goal, and expectancy theories. [AP] (Ch. 14, “14.3 Process Theories of Motivation”)

Operant conditioning links a stimulus, response, and consequence. Positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, and avoidance learning strengthen behaviour; nonreinforcement and punishment weaken it. Reinforcement may follow fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval, or variable-interval schedules. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.3 Process Theories of Motivation”)

Equity theory compares a person’s inputs and outcomes with those of a referent. Perceived underreward can produce seven stated responses: altering inputs, altering outcomes, cognitively distorting inputs or outcomes, leaving the field, acting on the referent, changing the referent, or rationalising the inequity. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.3 Process Theories of Motivation”)

Goal theory finds that difficult, specific, accepted goals accompanied by commitment and feedback can improve performance. Risks include narrowing attention, encouraging manipulation of measured results, and neglecting important work that is difficult to quantify. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.3 Process Theories of Motivation”)

Expectancy theory combines effort–performance expectancy, performance–outcome expectancy, and valence. Motivation weakens when employees doubt that effort can produce performance, doubt that performance will produce outcomes, or do not value the outcomes offered. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.3 Process Theories of Motivation”)

Recent research continues to support elements of several theories, especially goal processes, justice, and expectancy, while also showing that context and individual differences affect their operation. [AR] (Ch. 14, “14.4 Recent Research on Motivation Theories”)

### Chapter 15: Managing Teams

A team has a common purpose, performance goals, complementary skills, an agreed working approach, and mutual accountability. Unlike a conventional working group, it produces collective work products and distributes leadership as the work requires. [BT] (Ch. 15, “15.1 Teamwork in the Workplace”)

The source identifies eight practices for team effectiveness: establish urgency and direction; select members for skills; attend carefully to first meetings; set clear behavioural rules; create early performance-oriented tasks and goals; challenge the team with new information; spend substantial time together; and use positive feedback and recognition. [AP] (Ch. 15, “15.1 Teamwork in the Workplace”)

Eight cited contributors to collaboration include signature relationship practices, role models, a gift culture, training in relationship skills, a sense of community, ambitious goals, clearly defined roles, and building on existing relationships. [BT] (Ch. 15, “15.1 Teamwork in the Workplace”)

Tuckman’s original sequence contains forming, storming, norming, and performing; adjourning was added subsequently. The stages describe recurring developmental problems rather than a guaranteed one-way schedule. [BT] (Ch. 15, “15.2 Team Development Over Time”)

The source states this qualification directly: “The process of becoming a high-performance team is not a linear process.” [V] (Ch. 15, “15.2 Team Development Over Time”)

Team management involves persistent paradoxes: individual versus collective identity, support versus confrontation, performance versus learning, and managerial authority versus team autonomy. Effective teams manage these tensions rather than permanently eliminating one side. [AR] (Ch. 15, “15.3 Things to Consider When Managing Teams”)

Teams depend on stakeholders outside their formal boundaries. Boundary management includes acquiring information and resources, protecting the team, coordinating interdependencies, and maintaining sponsorship and legitimacy. [AP] (Ch. 15, “15.3 Things to Consider When Managing Teams”)

Conflict can damage trust and performance, but task-focused disagreement can expose assumptions and improve decisions. Lencioni’s source-attributed account links trust, productive conflict, commitment, accountability, and results; the text also describes “mining” for suppressed disagreement and granting real-time permission to challenge. [BT] (Ch. 15, “15.4 Opportunities and Challenges to Team Building”)

Team diversity can increase information and creativity while also increasing misunderstanding, categorisation, and conflict. Effects depend on leadership, inclusion, task type, climate, and the team’s capacity to integrate different perspectives. [BT] (Ch. 15, “15.5 Team Diversity”)

Multicultural teams commonly encounter four kinds of difference: direct versus indirect communication, accents and fluency, attitudes towards hierarchy, and conflicting decision-making norms. The source identifies four interventions: adaptation, structural intervention, managerial intervention, and exit. [BT] (Ch. 15, “15.6 Multicultural Teams”)

Cultural intelligence is represented through head, body, and heart: understanding, behavioural adaptation, and motivation or confidence. [BT] (Ch. 15, “15.6 Multicultural Teams”)

### Chapter 16: Managerial Communication

Communication involves a sender encoding a message, transmission through a channel, a receiver decoding it, and feedback, all under possible noise. Meaning is not simply transferred; it is interpreted through experience, context, language, and relationships. [AP] (Ch. 16, “16.1 The Process of Managerial Communication”)

The source identifies informational, corrective, and reinforcing feedback. Informational feedback reports results, corrective feedback directs adjustment, and reinforcing feedback supports desired behaviour. [AP] (Ch. 16, “16.1 The Process of Managerial Communication”)

Organisational communication may be oral, written, or nonverbal. Oral communication allows rapid interaction; written communication creates a more persistent record; and nonverbal cues can reinforce, qualify, or contradict words. [AP] (Ch. 16, “16.2 Types of Communications in Organizations”)

Communication is affected by social influences, perception, interaction involvement, emotional intelligence, and organisational design. Centralisation, hierarchy, role boundaries, and communication technology shape who can exchange information and how quickly it moves. [AP] (Ch. 16, “16.3 Factors Affecting Communications and the Roles of Managers”)

Mintzberg’s managerial roles are revisited as communication roles: figurehead, leader, and liaison; monitor, disseminator, and spokesperson; and entrepreneur, crisis handler, resource allocator, and negotiator. [BT] (Ch. 16, “16.3 Factors Affecting Communications and the Roles of Managers”)

Corporate identity is how an organisation presents and understands itself; reputation is how others evaluate it. Managerial language, decisions, actions, and consistency between claims and conduct shape reputation. [AP] (Ch. 16, “16.4 Managerial Communication and Corporate Reputation”)

The principal communication channels considered are talking, listening, reading, and writing. Cited estimates indicate that managers spend roughly three-quarters of their time communicating verbally and that talking and listening account for more than 78% of adults’ communication time. [BT] (Ch. 16, “16.5 The Major Channels of Management Communication Are Talking, Listening, Reading, and Writing”)

Listening requires attention, interpretation, evaluation, and response; it is not passive exposure to speech. Written communication requires clarity about audience, purpose, organisation, evidence, tone, and revision. [AP] (Ch. 16, “16.5 The Major Channels of Management Communication Are Talking, Listening, Reading, and Writing”)

The text rejects the assumption that data determine their own interpretation: “Information never speaks for itself.” [V] (Ch. 16, “16.5 The Major Channels of Management Communication Are Talking, Listening, Reading, and Writing”)

Facebook’s handling of user information is used to examine how communication practices, disclosure, privacy, organisational decisions, and public expectations combine to affect corporate reputation. [AE] (Ch. 16, “Critical Thinking Case”)

## Part VI: Planning, control, technology, and innovation

### Chapter 17: Organizational Planning and Controlling

Planning establishes goals and specifies how they will be attained. Plans contain outcome or goal statements describing desired ends and action statements describing the means of reaching them. [AP] (Ch. 17, “17.1 Is Planning Important”)

The source gives five reasons for planning: coping with uncertainty and change; focusing organisational activity; providing a coordinated roadmap; improving economic efficiency; and establishing standards for control. [AP] (Ch. 17, “17.1 Is Planning Important”)

Although managerial work is fragmented and much planning is mentally or conversationally performed, the source rejects the inference that managers do not plan. Empirical evidence associates formal planning with stronger organisational outcomes under suitable conditions. [AR] (Ch. 17, “17.1 Is Planning Important”)

The planning process has five stated stages: awareness of the current situation; establishment of outcome statements; premising; determining a course of action; and formulating supportive plans. [AP] (Ch. 17, “17.2 The Planning Process”)

Planning may be goal-directed, domain or directional, or hybrid. Goal planning specifies ends, domain planning specifies a field and direction without fully fixed ends, and hybrid planning combines both. [AP] (Ch. 17, “17.2 The Planning Process”)

The Deming cycle links planning and control through plan, do, check, and act. Results are compared with expectations, and the findings change subsequent plans and action. [BT] (Ch. 17, “17.2 The Planning Process”)

Plans are classified by five dimensions: hierarchical level, frequency of use, time frame, organisational scope, and contingency. The chapter distinguishes strategic, administrative, and operating plans; standing and single-use plans; short- and long-term plans; plans of differing scope; and contingency plans. [AP] (Ch. 17, “17.3 Types of Plans”)

Official goals communicate public and legitimating aspirations; operational goals guide actual activity. Goals direct attention, legitimise action, establish performance standards, and motivate organisational members. [AP] (Ch. 17, “17.4 Goals or Outcome Statements”)

Drucker’s source-attributed treatment argues that organisations need multiple goals covering areas such as market standing, innovation, productivity, profitability, resources, managerial development, employee performance, and public responsibility. [BT] (Ch. 17, “17.4 Goals or Outcome Statements”)

Effective goals are specific, difficult but attainable, accepted, supported by commitment, and accompanied by feedback. Goals can nevertheless encourage narrow attention, short-termism, gaming, or neglect of unmeasured responsibilities. [BT] (Ch. 17, “17.5 Formal Organizational Planning in Practice”; Ch. 17, “17.6 Employees’ Responses to Planning”)

The control process has four steps: establish standards; monitor ongoing performance; compare performance with standards; and evaluate results and take corrective action. [AP] (Ch. 17, “17.6 Employees’ Responses to Planning”)

Cybernetic control uses feedback and self-regulation, while noncybernetic control depends on external discretion. Precontrols act before work, concurrent controls act during it, and post-action controls operate after results; hybrid systems combine forms. [AP] (Ch. 17, “17.6 Employees’ Responses to Planning”)

Useful control information should be accurate, objective, timely, and accessible. Controls should focus on important activities and remain practical; excessive or misdirected control can reduce personal control, learning, motivation, and adaptive capacity. [AR] (Ch. 17, “17.6 Employees’ Responses to Planning”)

Management by objectives has four major components: specific goals; realistic and acceptable goals; joint participation in goal-setting, planning, and control; and feedback. Its effectiveness depends strongly on implementation and senior-management commitment. [BT] (Ch. 17, “17.7 Management by Objectives: A Planning and Control Technique”)

A review of 70 MBO cases found productivity gains in 68 and losses in two, with a mean increase exceeding 40%. The source cautions that results were strongest when top management was behaviourally as well as rhetorically committed. [BT] (Ch. 17, “17.7 Management by Objectives: A Planning and Control Technique”)

Control-oriented management relies more heavily on central direction and monitoring; involvement-oriented management distributes information, decision-making, capability, and rewards. The source treats involvement as a potential source of control through commitment and competence rather than the absence of accountability. [AR] (Ch. 17, “17.8 The Control- and Involvement-Oriented Approaches to Planning and Controlling”)

### Chapter 18: Management of Technology and Innovation

Technology is the organisational knowledge, processes, tools, and systems used to transform inputs into outputs. Management of technology and innovation plans, implements, evaluates, and controls technological capability so that it creates value and competitive advantage. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.1 MTI—Its Importance Now and In the Future”)

Four activities organise technology management: technology strategy, forecasting, roadmapping, and project-portfolio management. Together they connect technological possibilities with strategic choices, timing, investment, and risk. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.1 MTI—Its Importance Now and In the Future”)

The source distinguishes invention from innovation and product from process innovation. Management innovation changes how managerial work is organised or performed, not merely what product technology the firm sells. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.1 MTI—Its Importance Now and In the Future”)

Five “Cs” summarise innovation management: cast a wide net for ideas; create newness with existing products; create a culture open to new ideas; communicate knowledge; and change with courage. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.2 Developing Technology and Innovation”)

Six critical areas are identified: human resources, expansion through cooperation, internationalisation, environmental concerns, growth in services, and intellectual-property rights. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.2 Developing Technology and Innovation”)

Organisations must balance agility with efficiency. Four readiness capacities support adaptation: environmental sensing, communication and data systems, employee learning, and change management. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.2 Developing Technology and Innovation”)

Technology may be sourced externally, developed internally through research and development, or generated through entrepreneurial activity. External sourcing can accelerate access; internal development can strengthen ownership and learning; entrepreneurship can combine or commercialise knowledge in new ways. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.2 Developing Technology and Innovation”; Ch. 18, “18.3 External Sources of Technology and Innovation”; Ch. 18, “18.4 Internal Sources of Technology and Innovation”)

External forms include mergers and acquisitions, joint ventures, franchise agreements, licensing agreements, and formal or informal contracts. They differ in cost, control, integration, learning, and dependence on partners. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.3 External Sources of Technology and Innovation”)

Internal research and development offers greater ownership, organisational learning, and fit with existing capability, but it may be slow, expensive, uncertain, and dependent on key personnel. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.4 Internal Sources of Technology and Innovation”)

A value proposition asks which problem is being solved and why a customer should prefer the proposed solution. Lean start-up methods use experimentation and feedback to revise the proposition before committing resources at full scale. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.5 Management Entrepreneurship Skills for Technology and Innovation”)

Organisational learning distinguishes explicit knowledge that can be codified from tacit knowledge embedded in experience and practice. The Bessemer example shows how technological advance may depend on knowledge that is initially difficult to articulate or reproduce reliably. [BT] (Ch. 18, “18.6 Skills Needed for MTI”)

Technology forecasting is limited by complexity, discontinuity, interacting technologies, and uncertainty about adoption and use. Forecasts remain useful as structured inputs to judgement rather than certain predictions. [AR] (Ch. 18, “18.6 Skills Needed for MTI”)

Effective followership is characterised through five traits: independent critical thinking, active engagement, competence, courage, and self-management. Innovation leadership depends on capable followers as well as formal leaders. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.6 Skills Needed for MTI”)

Future-oriented technology management asks three questions: where the organisation is now, where it wants to be, and what it must do to move between those positions. [AP] (Ch. 18, “18.7 Managing Now for Future Technology and Innovation”)

Acer illustrates movement among internal innovation, alliances, acquisitions, and organisational spin-offs as technological and market conditions change. [AE] (Ch. 18, “18.7 Managing Now for Future Technology and Innovation”)

Novartis illustrates technology applied to an administrative process. Its IT community served 63,000 customers in 200 locations and 25 data centres; document-recognition software reduced manual invoice queries, and the project required a return on investment within nine months. [AE] (Ch. 18, “Critical Thinking Case”)

## Positions explicitly framed against

- **The classical functions as a complete description of managerial work.** The functions identify responsibilities, but observed managerial work is brief, fragmented, interaction-heavy, and dominated by communication. [AR] (Ch. 1, “1.3 Major Characteristics of the Manager’s Job”)
- **Complete rationality in decision-making.** Bounded rationality, time pressure, uncertainty, bias, and limited information make exhaustive optimisation uncommon. [BT] (Ch. 2, “2.4 Barriers to Effective Decision-Making”)
- **Escalating commitment merely because resources have already been spent.** Prior investment does not establish that continued investment is justified. [AR] (Ch. 2, “2.4 Barriers to Effective Decision-Making”)
- **A universal “one best way” to manage.** Systems and contingency perspectives make appropriate practice dependent on environmental and organisational conditions. [AR] (Ch. 3, “3.7 Contingency and System Management”)
- **SWOT as a sufficient strategic analysis.** Its broad categories require support from detailed external and internal analysis. [AR] (Ch. 8, “8.2 Using SWOT for Strategic Analysis”)
- **National culture as a deterministic description of individuals.** Within-country variation and contextual differences make rigid stereotyping unreliable. [AR] (Ch. 6, “6.4 Cultural Stereotyping and Social Institutions”)
- **Ethics as legal compliance alone.** The source treats legality, rights, consequences, justice, character, stakeholders, culture, and responsibility as related but non-identical considerations. [AR] (Ch. 5, “5.3 Ethical Principles and Responsible Decision-Making”; Ch. 5, “5.5 Ethics, Corporate Culture, and Compliance”)
- **CSR as philanthropy detached from operations.** Responsibility is linked to stakeholders, strategy, economic conduct, social effects, and environmental effects. [AR] (Ch. 5, “5.6 Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)”)
- **Change models as universally interchangeable recipes.** Model choice depends on scope, level, intentionality, participation, and uncertainty. [AR] (Ch. 10, “10.2 Organizational Change”; Ch. 10, “10.3 Managing Change”)
- **Diversity as an automatic cause of superior performance.** The evidence is mixed, and outcomes depend on inclusion, strategy, leadership, task, and integration. [AR] (Ch. 12, “12.3 Diversity and Its Impact on Companies”; Ch. 12, “12.6 Benefits and Challenges of Workplace Diversity”)
- **A universal leadership style.** Trait, behavioural, contingency, cross-cultural, substitute, and transformational perspectives all qualify such a claim. [AR] (Ch. 13, “13.4 The Trait Approach to Leadership”; Ch. 13, “13.6 Situational (Contingency) Approaches to Leadership”)
- **Maslow’s hierarchy as a rigid empirically settled sequence.** The source reports insufficient support for a universal fixed progression. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.2 Content Theories of Motivation”)
- **External rewards as invariably additive to intrinsic motivation.** Self-determination theory allows external controls to diminish intrinsic motivation. [BT] (Ch. 14, “14.2 Content Theories of Motivation”)
- **All conflict as harmful.** Relationship conflict is usually damaging, but well-managed task disagreement can improve analysis and expose assumptions. [AR] (Ch. 15, “15.4 Opportunities and Challenges to Team Building”)
- **Team development as a linear, irreversible sequence.** “The process of becoming a high-performance team is not a linear process.” [V] (Ch. 15, “15.2 Team Development Over Time”)
- **Information as self-interpreting.** “Information never speaks for itself.” [V] (Ch. 16, “16.5 The Major Channels of Management Communication Are Talking, Listening, Reading, and Writing”)
- **More control as invariably better.** Excessive control can reduce autonomy, learning, motivation, and perceived personal control. [AR] (Ch. 17, “17.6 Employees’ Responses to Planning”)
- **Technology acquisition as synonymous with internal invention.** The source treats external sourcing, internal research and development, and entrepreneurship as alternative and combinable paths. [AR] (Ch. 18, “18.2 Developing Technology and Innovation”)

## Citation and source-integrity notes

The source supplied for this reference is a 31,465-line Markdown rendering containing title and licence matter, the preface, eighteen chapters, chapter exercises and cases, references, and the complete index. All 31,465 lines were read; no partial-coverage caveat applies.

The front matter states both an original publication year of 2019 and copyright ©2026 Rice University. Those dates have been retained with their distinct meanings rather than collapsed into a single publication claim. The source identifies its textbook licence as Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial ShareAlike 4.0 International.

Section citations preserve the source’s chapter and section structure. Printed page headers survive in the Markdown, but section titles are used because they are more stable navigational locators in this representation.

Evidence markers are used in-band as follows: `[V]` is exact source wording; `[AP]` is a paraphrase of the source’s own exposition; `[AR]` reconstructs an argument made by the source; `[AE]` identifies an example or case used by the source; and `[BT]` identifies evidence, wording, statistics, or a framework that the source itself borrows or attributes to another named person or publication.

All `[V]` passages were checked character-for-character against the supplied Markdown. Formatting delimiters surrounding bold terms were not treated as part of the quoted prose, and no quotation was reconstructed from an unread source segment.

Names are attached to concepts only where the source itself makes that attribution in the cited passage. No biographical, historical, or conceptual attribution has been supplied from model training knowledge.

Quantitative claims retain the source’s own time and geographic context. In particular, WTO membership, workforce demographics, survey findings, legal summaries, and other externally sourced figures are reported as claims made in this textbook, not as independently updated facts current to 2026.

The source’s reference list and index were read for coverage and provenance, but they are not cited as primary evidence. Substantive claims are located in the chapter passages where OpenStax presents, applies, or attributes them.
